usage: Do you have time, by any chance?
Where is the restroom, by chance?
Are you Korean, by any chance?
examples: Is this seat free, by any chance?
혹시 영어 할 수 있는 분 계세요?
Is there anyone who can speak English, by chance?
Bring an umbrella, just in case.
nuance: 혹시 sits at the front of a question to soften it, like adding by any chance in English. It signals you are unsure and do not want to assume, so it makes requests and questions sound more polite and careful. The set phrase 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까 means just in case.
mistakes: Confusing 혹시 (by any chance) with 만약 (if/supposing)
Using 혹시 in plain statements instead of questions

examples: No way, is it already sold out?
설마 비 오는데 안 가는 건 아니죠?
Surely you're not skipping it just because it's raining?
I doubted it, but it was true.
설마 했는데 = I thought surely not, but
nuance: 설마 expresses strong doubt or disbelief that something bad or surprising could be true, like surely not or you've got to be kidding. It often leans negative, anticipating an answer of no. The phrase 설마 했는데 means I figured it couldn't be, but it was.
mistakes: Using 설마 for neutral guesses where 아마 (probably) fits
Forgetting that 설마 expects a denial, not a yes

usage: please, I hope it's not today
examples: Please be quiet, I'm begging you.
I really hope it doesn't rain, please.
Please let it slide just this once.
nuance: 제발 is a heartfelt please used when you are pleading or desperate, much stronger than the polite 주세요 ending alone. It carries real emotion, so save it for moments you truly want something, not routine requests. Pairing it with 좀 makes the plea sound even more urgent.
mistakes: Using 제발 for ordinary polite requests where 좀 is enough
Treating 제발 like the English filler please in every sentence

english: just in time; as it happens
usage: you came at just the right time
as it happens, I have time
I happen to be going that way too
examples: The bus came just then, so I didn't wait.
It happened to be on sale, so I bought one.
I was about to call, and just then they reached out.
nuance: 마침 marks a lucky or convenient coincidence, like just in time or as it happens, when timing works out in your favor. It frames an event as a happy accident rather than something planned. The phrase 마침 잘됐다 means that worked out perfectly.
mistakes: Confusing 마침 (luckily, just then) with 드디어 (finally)
Using 마침 for bad coincidences where 하필 fits better

english: of all times; why this one
usage: why right now of all times?
of all days it rained that day
of all things / of all people
examples: Of all days, I got sick on the day of the plans.
하필이면 비 오는 날 우산을 안 가져왔어요.
Of all days, I didn't bring an umbrella when it rained.
nuance: 하필 expresses frustration at unlucky or inconvenient timing, like of all times or why this one in particular. It is the negative twin of 마침: where 마침 is lucky, 하필 is the annoying coincidence. The emphatic form 하필이면 stresses just how unfortunate the choice of time or person feels.
mistakes: Using 하필 for good luck where 마침 belongs
Dropping the complaining tone that 하필 always carries

english: after a long while; for once
usage: we met after a long time
examples: I was excited to meet my friend after so long.
It's a rare day off, but it's raining.
Since we're out for once, let's eat something good.
nuance: 모처럼 marks something that happens rarely and is therefore precious, like after a long while or for once. It adds a sense of let's make the most of this because it doesn't come often. It frequently pairs with a slight letdown, as in a rare day off that gets rained out.
mistakes: Using 모처럼 for everyday routine events
Confusing 모처럼 (rare and welcome) with 오랜만에, which is more neutral

usage: this is the little that's left
examples: I was late, but at least I caught the last train.
The pay is low, but at least there's no overtime.
At least I have you, thank goodness.
nuance: 그나마 points to a small consolation in an otherwise bad or limited situation, like at least or even that little bit. It acknowledges things aren't great but highlights the one redeeming part. With 그나마 다행이다 it becomes the common phrase at least that's a relief.
mistakes: Using 그나마 when the situation is fully positive
Mixing up 그나마 with 그래도 (still / even so)

examples: 어쩌면 이번 주말에 시간이 날 수도 있어요.
Maybe I'll have some free time this weekend.
어쩌면 우리 전에 만난 적 있을지도 몰라요.
어쩌면 그 사람 말이 맞을지도 몰라요.
nuance: 어쩌면 means maybe or possibly and opens up a genuine but uncertain possibility, often one the speaker hadn't fully considered. It pairs naturally with the guessing ending -ㄹ지도 모르다. Compared with 아마 (probably), 어쩌면 feels more open-ended and less confident.
mistakes: Treating 어쩌면 as certain like 아마 (probably)
Pairing 어쩌면 with a flat assertion instead of a guessing ending

english: as many as; no less than
usage: for no less than ten years
examples: That bag costs a whopping three million won.
I stood in line for a full two hours.
이 영화를 무려 천만 명이 봤어요.
No less than ten million people saw this movie.
nuance: 무려 goes right before a number to stress that the amount is surprisingly large, like a whopping or no less than. It signals the speaker finds the figure impressive or shocking. It only works with quantities, not with general statements.
mistakes: Using 무려 without a number or amount after it
Confusing 무려 with 약 (approximately), which softens rather than amplifies

examples: 그 식당은 맛있고, 심지어 가격도 싸요.
That restaurant is tasty, and on top of that it's cheap.
It was raining, and I didn't even have an umbrella.
그 사람은 심지어 내 이름도 기억 못 해요.
That person doesn't even remember my name.
nuance: 심지어 introduces an extreme or surprising addition, like even or on top of that, pushing a point further than expected. It often pairs with the particle 도 (also/even) on the following word. Use it to escalate, whether the extra fact is good or bad.
mistakes: Confusing 심지어 (even, going further) with 게다가 (moreover), which is more neutral
Forgetting the 도 particle that usually follows

usage: I can't understand it at all
examples: I can't figure out this problem no matter what.
It's so spicy I just can't eat it.
There's no way I can make time.
nuance: 도저히 means by no means or no matter how hard one tries, and it must be paired with a negative like 못, 안, or -ㄹ 수 없다. It conveys that something is utterly impossible after real effort. Without a negative the sentence is ungrammatical.
mistakes: Using 도저히 in a positive sentence (it requires a negative)
Swapping in 절대 (never/absolutely), which can also negate but sounds more like a vow

examples: Rather than wait, walking would be faster.
복잡한 데 가느니 차라리 집에서 쉴래요.
I'd sooner rest at home than go somewhere crowded.
택시비 낼 바엔 차라리 일찍 나올게요.
Rather than pay for a taxi, I'll just leave early.
nuance: 차라리 picks the lesser of two undesirable options, like I'd rather or I'd sooner, when neither choice is ideal. It often follows the pattern -느니 (rather than doing X) to set up the comparison. The tone is resigned: not a happy choice, just the more bearable one.
mistakes: Using 차라리 when you actually want the option (it implies neither is great)
Forgetting it usually compares against a worse alternative
